summary: Jude is a short and forceful letter. The author intended to write about the salvation we share, but changed subject to warn against people who had slipped into the community and turned grace into a pretext for immorality. He draws on examples of judgment from the Scriptures and from Jewish traditions (the people in the wilderness, the rebellious angels, Sodom and Gomorrah, Cain, Balaam and Korah) and quotes a prophecy attributed to Enoch. He closes with counsel of mercy and with one of the best-known doxologies of the New Testament.
name: The title “of Jude” (Iouda) comes from the author's name, the Greek form of Judah; English Bibles call him Jude to distinguish him from Judas Iscariot, with whom he has no connection. Some traditions identify him with the apostle Judas Thaddaeus, an identification many do not accept.
facts: 26th book of the New Testament; 7th and last of the General (or Catholic) Epistles

structure.title: Greeting and reason
structure.text: Jude greets those who are called and explains why he writes: it is necessary to contend for the faith, because ungodly people have crept in unnoticed (1:1–4).

structure.title: Examples of judgment
structure.text: The people who did not believe in the wilderness, the angels who abandoned their dwelling and Sodom and Gomorrah show that God judges (1:5–7).

structure.title: Portrait of the intruders
structure.text: Compared to Cain, Balaam and Korah, to clouds without water and trees without fruit; Enoch's prophecy announces judgment on them (1:8–16).

structure.title: Exhortation and doxology
structure.text: Remembering the words of the apostles, building oneself up in the faith, showing mercy to those who doubt and praising God, who is able to keep from stumbling (1:17–25).

extra.title: Books beyond the Hebrew canon
extra.text: Jude expressly quotes a prophecy of Enoch (1:14–15), which corresponds to a passage of 1 Enoch, a Jewish work preserved complete in Ethiopic and in Aramaic fragments found at Qumran. The dispute between the archangel Michael and the devil over the body of Moses (1:9) is not in the Old Testament; ancient writers, such as Origen, linked it to a work called the Assumption of Moses, now known only in part. This use caused doubts about the letter in some places in the early Church, as Jerome and Eusebius record.

writing.tradition: The author is identified as Jude, brother of James and, therefore, one of the brothers of Jesus mentioned in the Gospels (Mark 6:3). According to Hegesippus, quoted by Eusebius, grandsons of Jude were still living in Galilee in the time of Domitian. The letter was accepted early in several churches (it appears in the Muratorian Canon and is used by Tertullian and Clement of Alexandria), but, because of the quotation of Enoch, it was questioned by some and is among the disputed books in Eusebius's list.
writing.academic: Scholars are divided. Many accept that the letter comes from Jude, the brother of Jesus, or from his circle, in a Jewish-Christian setting in or near Palestine, and date it between 50 and 90. Many others see it as written in Jude's name, at the end of the 1st century, noting the reference to the faith “once for all entrusted” and to the words spoken “by the apostles” (1:3; 1:17) as things of the past. There is broad agreement that 2 Peter 2 depends on Jude.

context: The letter assumes readers familiar with the Scriptures of Israel and with Jewish traditions that circulated outside them, such as those of 1 Enoch, which suggests a Jewish-Christian setting. The intruders take part in the community's love feasts (the agape meals, 1:12), reject authority, seek advantage and divide the community (1:19). The text does not say where the recipients were.
places: Sodom and Gomorrah and the surrounding cities
themes: the faith entrusted to the saints
